Publisher XML converted to located text (jats_text); it holds the title, an empty §0 Abstract heading, and the figure and table captions only, with no body paragraphs
pages_convention: Mixed. Figure and table captions are cited by their XML caption label exactly as printed ('Fig. 5', 'Table 3'). Body text is cited by PDF pages counted from 1, which equal the printed journal pages 1-18, because the supplied XML text contains no body paragraphs. entry.evidence: The exact cause of these strong seismic amplitudes is still not fully understood, although seismic anisotropy and hydrothermal alteration are often invoked as key contributors.

steps.action: The authors pose three objectives: document P- and S-wave velocities across the deposit, discriminate crack-induced from CPO-born anisotropy at depth, and evaluate whether seismic reflection can identify the shear zone.
steps.quote: evaluate the feasibility of using seismic reflection to identify gold-hosting structures, such as the Thunderbox shear zone

steps.action: From published laboratory studies they take the postulate that texture-related (CPO) velocity anisotropy, rather than cracks, causes strong reflections from deep deformation zones.
steps.quote: seismic velocity anisotropy associated with the texture of a rock is the key causative factor

steps.action: They measured ultrasonic Vp, Vs and bulk density axially and radially on 126 cores from seven lithologies, and XRD mineralogy, grain density and porosity on 11 representative samples.
steps.quote: Ultrasonic P- and S-wave velocities (Vp and Vs) were measured at ambient conditions along the axis of the 126 core samples

steps.action: Four resampled plugs (two talc-schist shear-zone samples, one dacite, one mafic volcaniclastic) were placed in a triaxial cell with 16 P-wave transducers and cycled in confining pressure from 0 to 65 MPa, standing in for depths to about 1500 m.
steps.quote: It was subjected to a stepwise increase in confining pressure in increments of 2.5 MPa up to 65 MPa

steps.action: They checked the homogeneity premise of the anisotropy estimation with X-ray CT images and repeated Vp measurements at several heights and azimuths; the spread is within experimental uncertainty.
steps.quote: The small variability in Vp observed for a given propagation direction at multiple locations indicates that the samples are approximately homogeneous

steps.action: They compared ambient impedances on Vp- and Vs-density plots against the 0.06 reflectivity detection limit; only massive basalt and the anisotropic talc schist stand out, and dacite alteration levels cannot be told apart.
steps.quote: seismic reflectivity cannot discriminate different dacite alteration levels

steps.action: They recorded Vp against confining pressure along more than 100 ray paths; shear-zone velocities rise most across the foliation and level off above 10-20 MPa, and hysteresis is weak.
steps.quote: this result suggests that the microcracks are nearly closed at pressures above 20 MPa

steps.action: They ran an unconstrained inversion of the redundant Vp data for Thomsen's alpha, epsilon, delta and the orientation of the symmetry axis; it did not converge and gave inconsistent axis orientations.
steps.quote: This unconstrained inversion was unstable, i.e., lack of convergence

steps.action: They fixed the orientation of the symmetry axis from the CT foliation and the slowest Vp directions, then re-inverted at each pressure step; alpha rises and epsilon falls up to about 20 MPa, and delta stays poorly resolved (about ±0.25).
steps.quote: the inversion of the velocity data was then carried out with a fixed orientation of the elastic symmetry axis

steps.action: They measured bulk CPO pole figures of chlorite, talc, dolomite and quartz in the two shear-zone samples by neutron diffraction (KOWARI, ANSTO).
steps.quote: Chlorite (CC) and talc (T) have the strongest CPO in the samples

steps.action: They computed the crack-free, CPO-only Vp distribution with MTEX (single-crystal stiffness tensors and a Hill average), giving AVp of about 18% for sample A and 22.5% for sample B.
steps.quote: The strong CPO of chlorite and talc results in high AVp

steps.action: From the four pressurized samples they estimated that ambient Vp extrapolates to in situ conditions by an increase of about 4-5%, except for strongly cracked samples.
steps.quote: extrapolated to the conditions at depth by an increase of 4 to 5%

steps.action: They computed isotropic and anisotropic (Ruger 1997) P-wave reflection coefficients against incidence angle and depth for the dacite/shear zone A and B interfaces, using the inverted Thomsen parameters.
steps.quote: the evolution of the P-wave reflection coefficient with depth (pressures) across the Thunderbox shear zone is estimated using Ruger (1997)

steps.action: They compared the anisotropic curves with the isotropic baseline and with the detection limit: anisotropy changes reflectivity strongly above 30 degrees, and normal-incidence reflectivity near 0.06 decreases with depth.
steps.quote: the anisotropy parameters obtained from the samples of the shear zone dramatically affect seismic reflectivity for incident angles higher than 30⁰

steps.action: Using the flat pressure-velocity curves above 20 MPa and the weak hysteresis, they set aside microcracks as the main source of shear-zone anisotropy below about 400 m.
steps.quote: the effects of cracks on the velocities diminish significantly at pressures above 20 MPa

steps.action: They compared CPO-derived velocities with laboratory velocities at 65 MPa; maximum velocities and spatial distribution are similar, but measured anisotropy is higher, which they attribute to unclosed cracks and input uncertainty.
steps.quote: it is clear that (i) CPO is a significant source of seismic anisotropy in the analyzed samples from the shear zone

steps.action: They swapped the biotite (phlogopite) stiffness tensor from Chheda et al. (2014) to Wenk et al. (2012); the velocity distribution is similar, but AVp of sample B drops from 22.5% to 15%.
steps.quote: the overall P-wave anisotropy reduces from 22.5% when using Chheda et al. (2014)

steps.action: Holding the measured CPO fixed, they varied talc, chlorite and biotite fractions over the observed ranges, with quartz and dolomite fixed at 20% or 10%; anisotropy tracks talc and biotite content.
steps.quote: we varied the amount of talc (10%-53%), chlorite (14%-60%), and biotite (0%-27%)

steps.action: They conclude that the CPO of phyllosilicates, especially talc, is the main source of shear-zone anisotropy, that this anisotropy significantly affects reflectivity, and that shear-zone reflectivity falls with depth.
steps.quote: the main source of seismic anisotropy observed on samples from the shear zone is the CPO of the phyllosilicates minerals, especially talc

tree.answer: Strong reflectors along deep shear zones; high anisotropy of talc-schist shear-zone rocks
Velocities and density measured directly; Thomsen parameters only through inversion
Document velocities, separate crack from CPO anisotropy, judge seismic detectability of the shear zone
Crack anisotropy is pressure-sensitive; CPO anisotropy is pressure-insensitive and predictable from texture
Set: confining pressure 0-65 MPa applied in the laboratory
Partly: two shear-zone samples, stiffness-tensor swap and mineral-fraction variation; no field data
CPO is the main source of anisotropy; cracks are secondary below about 400 m

end.claim: Below about 400 m (above 20 MPa), the high P-wave anisotropy of the Thunderbox talc-schist shear zone comes mainly from the CPO of phyllosilicates, especially talc, rather than from microcracks.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the neutron-diffraction CPO-derived velocities with velocities measured at 65 MPa, together with the pressure-insensitivity above 20 MPa, is what allows the anisotropy to be attributed to CPO rather than cracks.

gates.evidence: Action: the crack-versus-CPO question directed which two shear-zone samples went to pressure testing and neutron diffraction (p. 2-3), but the operator set the sample supply and allowed only four cores to be resampled (p. 3). Claim: the CPO-derived velocities could have disagreed with the measured ones; they match in maximum and distribution, while the anisotropy mismatch is explained post hoc by cracks and input uncertainty (p. 14). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen; the inversion constraint was added after the unconstrained run failed (p. 9-10).

imports.item: Neutron diffraction texture measurement (KOWARI diffractometer, ANSTO)
Medical X-ray CT scanner used to image the core plugs
Texture analysis and J-index (Bunge 1982); MTEX toolbox for texture-derived properties
Hill (1952) average of effective elastic moduli
Ab initio and experimental single-crystal stiffness tensors (talc, chlorite, phlogopite)

novelty_claims.quote: To our knowledge, only few studies have reported experimental estimation of elastic anisotropy in deformational zones associated with metallic ore deposits.
This study provides data of seismic properties, such as P-wave velocities and anisotropy, S-wave velocities, and density that are rare at mineral deposits

limits: The supplied XML text contains only the captions, so body steps are located by PDF page; the XML-locator convention could not be followed for the body. No review file or earlier version was supplied, so there is no review sequence. The entry could also be read as external_goal: the operator supplied the cores to plan a future survey (p. 2). The operator restricted the pressure and CPO work to four and two samples, so the CPO claim rests on two plugs from one drill core. Vs was not measured under pressure, and beta for the reflectivity model was scaled from the ambient Vp/Vs ratio (p. 13). Delta is poorly resolved (±0.25). The symmetry axis was fixed by visual inspection after the unconstrained inversion failed. No field seismic or log data test the reflectivity predictions. The phrase 'seismic survey data' on p. 12 appears to refer to laboratory data (inference). Sub-claims and their statuses: reflectivity between most lithologies lies below the 0.06 detection limit (estimate_with_resolution); anisotropy significantly changes reflectivity above 30 degrees incidence (modelled expectation, no observational test); ambient Vp scales to in situ by 4-5% (estimate_with_resolution, four samples); surface seismic is unsuitable and VSP or MSP is preferred (recommendation, untested). Composition is none_fits: the paper is mainly a property-characterization case study with one embedded two-rival test (cracks versus CPO) under laboratory-set conditions; it is not a full strong-inference walk, a trace series, or capability-first.

disagreements.target: Ji and Salisbury (1993); Schmitt (2015): microcracks fully closed only above 200 MPa
disagreements.support: Flat Vp-pressure curves above about 20 MPa and weak hysteresis suggest crack effects become minor well below 200 MPa.
disagreements.quote: [...] report that the cracks are fully closed only at pressures higher than 200 MPa

disagreements.target: Mine geologists' lithological classification of the 'mafic volcaniclastic' pressurized sample
disagreements.support: XRD finds 22% quartz and no pyroxene or amphibole, and bulk and grain densities are like those of a felsic rock.
disagreements.quote: cast significant doubt if it was classified correctly by the geologist of the mine

disagreements.target: Wenk et al. (2012) phlogopite stiffness tensor
disagreements.support: Using it lowers modelled AVp to 15%, further from the measured value than with Chheda et al. (2014); the authors attribute this to differing symmetry and composition.
disagreements.quote: This may be attributed to the different crystal symmetry and chemical composition of phlogopite published by Wenk et al (2012)

disagreements.target: Position that seismic methods can identify gold-hosting structures (Drummond et al., 2000)
disagreements.support: Reflectivity modelling, together with the steep dip and limited width of the structures, indicates surface seismic is unlikely to detect the Thunderbox shear zone at depth.
disagreements.quote: the surface seismic survey is not the most suitable seismic technique for detecting the mineralization and the shear zone at the Thunderbox Gold Mine

alternatives_considered.chosen: Inversion with the symmetry-axis orientation fixed from CT foliation and slowest Vp
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Unconstrained inversion with unknown symmetry axis
alternatives_considered.reason: The unconstrained inversion was unstable because of multiple local minima

alternatives_considered.chosen: Ambient Vp/Vs ratio as the a priori input to the inversion
alternatives_considered.reason: No Vs under pressure; results are insensitive to this value (Nadri et al., 2012)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Full monoclinic phlogopite stiffness tensor of Chheda et al. (2014) for biotite
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Pseudo-hexagonal biotite tensor (Aleksandrov and Ryzhova, 1961); phlogopite tensor of Wenk et al. (2012)
alternatives_considered.reason: True monoclinic symmetry; result closer to the measured anisotropy at 65 MPa

alternatives_considered.chosen: Report only the pressurization branch of the pressure cycle
alternatives_considered.reason: The two branches are similar within experimental uncertainty (weak hysteresis)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Model only the dacite/shear zone interface, with dacite taken as isotropic
alternatives_considered.reason: Dacite and mafic volcaniclastic have similar velocities under pressure
